Designing and Evaluating Factuality Indicators for LLM-based Chatbots Thanks: *Work conducted while at Meta CCS: Human-centered computing Empirical studies in HCI Greta Warren email: grwa@di.ku.dk Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, University of Copenhagen , Copenhagen , Denmark , Jessica Heal email: jfh@openai.com Affiliation: OpenAI , USA Affiliation: Meta Platforms, Inc. , Menlo Park , California , USA , Sila Eser email: silaeser.design@gmail.com Affiliation: Meta Platforms, Inc. , Menlo Park , California , USA , Denise M. Leto email: denisemleto@gmail.com Affiliation: Meta Platforms, Inc. , Menlo Park , California , USA , Christine M. Lehane email: christine.m.lehane@gmail.com Affiliation: Meta Platforms, Inc. , Menlo Park , California , USA and Isabelle Augenstein email: augenstein@di.ku.dk Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, University of Copenhagen , Copenhagen , Denmark Abstract. Generative AI systems increasingly mediate how people seek information, yet communicating AI factuality to laypeople remains challenging. Through a mixed-methods investigation involving interviews (N=8), a survey (N=1,000), and an experiment (N=5,151), we examine how people evaluate AI-generated information for gardening, mathematical, and medical queries, and how factuality indicators (confidence and sources) shape perceptions. Our interviews and survey show people selectively verify AI responses using external and AI-provided evidence, moderated by contextual factors. Although confidence-indicators affected trust and accuracy perceptions, people hold diverse, ambiguous interpretations of AI confidence. Sources were viewed as crucial, yet users raised concerns about source reliability and verification effort. Our experiment showed that confidence and source-based indicators influenced initial perceptions, but effects disappeared once participants learned the response’s correctness. Medical queries elicited skepticism regardless of indicator. Findings motivate helping users interpret model confidence and integrating source information into the interface to support calibrated trust in AI-supported information-seeking. Keywords: human-AI interaction, information-seeking, conversational interface, trust, factuality, mixed methods 1. Introduction Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as tools for information-seeking ( Simon et al., 2025 ; Ceron et al., 2026 ) due to their growing prominence in online search and social media platforms ( Grossman et al., 2026 ; Kirsten et al., 2026 ) , and conversational interfaces. Yet the fluency of LLM-generated responses does not guarantee their factuality: models can produce plausible-sounding but inaccurate, hallucinated text that is not reliably grounded in any verifiable source ( Pauli et al., 2025 ; Augenstein et al., 2024 ; Ji et al., 2023 ) , which can lead people to follow misleading advice. Prior work has explored two main approaches to helping users assess the factuality of AI-generated responses: communicating the model’s own confidence ( Kim et al., 2024 ; Prabhudesai et al., 2023 ; Bhatt et al., 2021 ; Vasconcelos et al., 2025 ) , and providing sources or citations that allow a claim to be independently checked ( Kim et al., 2025 ; Warren et al., 2026 ) . While these approaches are promising, findings suggest that their impacts depend heavily on how the information is presented, and it is unclear how such indicators should be designed. As AI chatbots take on a larger role in how people access and act on information, understanding how everyday users evaluate and make decisions about when to trust an AI-generated response is essential to designing systems. However, large-scale studies assessing people’s verification behaviours and attitudes are scarce, making it difficult to design effective factuality indicators for everyday chatbot usage. Furthermore, most empirical studies have been focused on specific tasks, such as fact-checking ( Warren et al., 2026 ) , however, people increasingly use AI chatbots for everyday personal questions related to hobbies, work, and health. Comparatively little is known about how everyday LLM chatbot users perceive and interpret confidence- and source-based indicators. To address these gaps, we posed the following research questions: RQ1: How should factuality indicators be designed to help people assess AI factuality? RQ2: How do laypeople assess the factuality of information from AI chatbots? RQ3: How do factuality indicators affect perceptions of AI chatbots? We address these questions through a mixed-methods approach comprising three complementary studies. First, we conducted in-depth interviews with eight AI users to surface how they perceive AI confidence, sources, and verification behaviours ( RQ1 ), as well as their reactions to speculative design concepts for factuality indicators. Second, we conducted a nationally representative survey of 1,000 U.S. AI users to characterise how, when, and why people currently verify information from AI chatbots, and what additional information and support might be useful ( RQ2 ). Third, we conducted a large-scale between-participants experiment (N=5,151) that systematically varied the type of factuality indicator shown (confidence-labels, confidence-percentages, confidence-bubbles, source-labels, sources and confidence language, and no indicator), the topic of the query (gardening, mathematics, medical advice), and the correctness of the response, to evaluate how different factuality indicators influence perceived accuracy, information sufficiency, trust, and sentiment, both before and after participants learned whether the response was actually correct ( RQ3 ). Our interviews revealed that while users value confidence indicators, they hold diverse and often conflicting interpretations of what confidence means. Sources were perceived as highly important, given that they provide evidence that can be independently evaluated, although users also described the effort and other limitations associated with source verification. Our survey showed that most people verify AI responses at least some of the time, but they primarily do so through external information seeking and source inspection rather than through AI-provided confidence information. Finally, our experiment found that both confidence and source indicators have a small effect on people’s perceptions of an AI chatbot before a response’s correctness is known, yet this effect dissipates once the correct response is revealed. We further find that contextual factors, particularly the stakes associated with a task, influence the effectiveness of factuality indicators. 2. Related Work 2.1. Assessing AI factuality Although LLM chatbots can produce fluent, convincing outputs, they often also produce false information that can mislead their users and others ( Ji et al., 2023 ; Augenstein et al., 2024 ) . This can lead people to erroneously trust or follow AI advice, often termed overreliance ( Ibrahim et al., 2025 ) , which can lead to inaccurate decisions, skill erosion, and other potential harms ( Miller, 2023 ; Buçinca et al., 2025 ) . The superficially plausible and persuasive nature of LLM outputs makes it important to be able to distinguish factual information from false information, and so recent work in human-AI interaction has explored methods of supporting AI users to assess the factuality (that is, a response that is truthful, or based on fact ( Augenstein et al., 2024 ; Ji et al., 2023 ; Do et al., 2025 ) ), of an AI response, so that they can decide whether or not the response is trustworthy ( Lee and See, 2004 ) . Recent work has shown that factuality indicators, that is, design features that provide the user with additional information to assist with evaluating the factuality of a response, can be useful supports and help people to appropriately calibrate their reliance on AI advice. For example, Do et al. ( Do et al., 2025 ) show that incorporating in-line highlighting in LLM responses based on factuality levels made it easier for users to validate the accuracy of the LLM’s response and increased their trust, compared to a baseline where no style was applied. Another study found that highlighting uncertain parts of the model output did reduce overreliance, but also made people more likely to reject correct AI responses ( Bo et al., 2025 ) , while other approaches have shown that removing factually incorrect information from responses can enhance user trust ( Do and Geyer, 2025 ) . Although various methods of signalling the factuality of AI responses have been studied, it remains unclear how these various methods are understood and used by people in everyday interactions with AI chatbots across various contexts. In this paper, we study two prominent categories of factuality indicators for LLM-based chatbots – confidence and source indicators – in order to understand how they impact people’s perceptions of accuracy and trust in AI, and how they can be designed to more effectively support people in AI-supported information-seeking. 2.2. Effects of communicating confidence and uncertainty Various methods of communicating AI uncertainty to human users have been proposed with the aim of allowing people to better calibrate their trust and reliance in human-AI decision-making ( Bhatt et al., 2021 ; Chiaburu et al., 2024 ) . For example, pre-LLM work has found that presenting numerical confidence (e.g., percentages) to users can improve task performance ( Bansal et al., 2021 ) and trust calibration ( Zhang et al., 2020 ) . Confidence estimates and explanations have been found to have complementary effects on people’s accuracy in predicting a model’s output ( Papantonis and Belle, 2025 ) , while other work has found that automatically highlighting snippets of code that are likely to be edited helped programmers to complete their tasks faster and were subjectively preferred ( Vasconcelos et al., 2025 ) . Visualising AI uncertainty has also been proposed as a method of getting people to slow down and think more deliberatively ( Prabhudesai et al., 2023 ) . Although these methods facilitate precise, granular uncertainty quantification, they can be challenging for people to interpret ( Hofman et al., 2020 ) and put into action ( Warren et al., 2025 ) . Uncertainty communicated through natural language may be more intuitively understood, though people also differ in how they interpret them (e.g., individual differences for what people consider “very confident” tend to be large) ( Steyvers et al., 2025 ; Belém et al., 2024 ; Wallsten et al., 1993 ; Zimmer, 1983 ) . Recent work in LLM-specific settings has found that how an LLM verbalises uncertainty in its own generated text (e.g., by prepending statements like “I’m not sure, but…”) shapes both reliance and trust ( Kim et al., 2024 ) . However, the same study also found that people’s perceptions and behaviours are highly sensitive to how such verbalised uncertainty is phrased. It remains unclear how different styles of confidence indicators shape people’s perceptions of AI chatbots, and how they should be designed to support factuality assessment more effectively. In this study, we address this by examining how people interpret various sorts of confidence indicators (numerical percentages, categorical labels, and natural language) and systematically comparing how they impact perceptions and trust in AI responses. 2.3. Effects of providing sources, evidence and citations An intersecting line of research has examined how providing sources in various forms alongside a generated response can support people to assess AI factuality. Presenting sources in the form of citations or links has become a common design pattern in commercial LLMs (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini), however these approaches are not always reliable: they can misrepresent the original source (e.g., ( Liu et al., 2023 ) ) as well as fabricate non-existent sources (e.g., ( Alkaissi and McFarlane, 2023 ) ). Kim et al. ( Kim et al., 2025 ) found that providing sources alongside AI responses made people more confident in their responses in an AI-supported information-seeking task and appeared to increase the credibility of the LLM response. They also found that verifying the sources increased people’s performance in determining when they could or could not rely on the AI system’s answer, though it did not eliminate overreliance entirely. However, some studies have shown that people often do not verify sources when provided as clickable links to external information ( Kim et al., 2024 ) , while other studies indicated that presenting evidence from sources in a more integrated way (e.g., dropdown buttons) can improve people’s engagement with sources when evaluating whether a fact-checking claim is true or false ( Warren et al., 2026 ) . This evidence suggests that the way in which sources are presented to users plays a significant role in their verification behaviour. However, the best approaches to designing source indicators to support factuality assessment are unclear. Furthermore, much of the existing literature focuses on tasks in which participants must evaluate AI responses focused on general knowledge or fact-checking question-answering, rather than on everyday LLM chatbot users who are concerned with specific personal queries. In the current paper, we examine the role of sources in people’s verification behaviour, how they determine source credibility, and how providing sources alongside AI responses impacts people’s perceived accuracy, trust, information sufficiency and impressions of an AI chatbot, across a variety of topics, ranging from benign everyday queries to high stakes medical ones. 3. RQ1: How should factuality indicators be designed to help people assess AI factuality? To investigate and develop an initial understanding of how laypeople perceive and reason about AI factuality cues, including confidence indicators and source-based verification features, we conducted an exploratory qualitative study with AI chatbot users. 3.1. Method We conducted semi-structured interviews to enable participants to articulate existing mental models of accuracy, trust, and verification while providing detailed feedback on a set of speculative design concepts. Interviews were conducted in March 2025. 3.1.1. Participants. Eight participants from the United States were recruited to participate in one-on-one virtual interviews (see Table 1 for an overview of demographics). All participants reported experience using generative AI tools either weekly or daily. Participant ID Gender Age AI Usage P1 Female 29 Weekly P2 Female 23 Daily P3 Female 23 Weekly P4 Male 17 Daily P5 Male 25 Daily P6 Male 27 Daily P7 Male 17 Weekly P8 Female 16 Weekly Table 1. Interview participant demographics 3.1.2. Interview Protocol. Each participant completed a 60-minute remote interview. Sessions were audio-recorded. Interviews began with a warm-up discussion about how participants used AI, and how much they relied on them. The main interview focused on five topics: (1) Current behaviours and expectations around information accuracy: Participants were asked about how they assessed the accuracy of information from (i) people they knew, (ii) news and social media, and (iii) AI tools. Questions focused on what evidence they expected to be provided, how they determined source credibility, and how sources (could) present indicators of credibility or accuracy. (2) Communicating AI accuracy: Participants were prompted to imagine how AI confidence could be communicated in a useful way, and react to design stimuli illustrating AI confidence indicators such as labels and percentages. Participants were also asked what they considered acceptable levels of confidence, and what they interpreted such confidence labels to be based on. (3) Using confidence indicators: Questions focused on how AI factuality indicators might be useful to them, and what additional information and explanations they might require. Participants were then asked to react to further design stimuli showcasing additional information about sources or confidence and discuss their utility and preferences. (4) Citations and sources: Participants were asked about their experiences with AI-provided sources and their verification behaviours. They were shown design stimuli showing examples of how source information could be provided (e.g., pop-ups or inline with responses) and asked to evaluate them and imagine how they could be used and improved. (5) Contextual factors: Participants were asked to imagine how they would react in certain situations, such as if an AI chatbot’s response was labelled with ’low accuracy’, or if a confidence indicator was misaligned with the actual accuracy, as well as about how specific topics or situations might impact how important or useful AI factuality indicators would be. Finally, participants were asked for any further thoughts or comments they had. Throughout the interview, participants were asked follow-up questions, and encouraged to explain their reasoning, describe their expectations about what an AI chatbot should do, and compare alternatives. 3.1.3. Design Stimuli. We created a set of design concept images which were presented during the interviews to elicit participant reactions, expectations, and explore other possible approaches for communicating AI factuality. We designed the images to show a conversation with an AI chatbot on a mobile device, to resemble a scenario in which people use AI to seek information for a medical query. We chose this medical context to prompt people to reflect on how to assess AI factuality for a high-stakes topic, similar to previous work (e.g., ( Kim et al., 2024 ) ). The content consisted of a two-turn interaction with the chatbot, in which the user first makes a query about side-effects of a medication, and the chatbot response probes for more information. The response is accompanied by a high confidence indicator. Then, the user responds to the follow-up question, and the chatbot provides a response, this time with a low confidence indicator. All participants were shown the same design concepts, but the order of different options for the same concept was randomised between participants (e.g., one participant saw the options in Fig 1 in the order: Option 3, Option 1, Option 2, Option 4). Design Stimulus A (see Fig. 1 ) presented four different versions of AI chatbot confidence indicators: (i) Confidence-labels (high/low), (ii) Confidence-percentage (85%/30%), (iii) Confidence-labels with inline dropdown (check mark / warning symbol and dropdown arrow), and (iv) Confidence-aligned language (“reliable sources agree” vs “I can’t confirm this information”). We chose these four indicator types to exemplify different approaches: confidence labels for categorical assessment, confidence percentages for quantitative, more granular information, dropdown for providing additional detail on demand, and confidence-aligned language for a more natural conversational indicator as opposed to specific interface details. Design Stimulus B (see Fig. 13 ) showed percentages underneath the AI responses with three different candidate labels: confidence, reliability, and certainty, to understand how different linguistic framings shaped people’s interpretations of AI-generated information and gauge preferences. Each design was otherwise identical. Design Stimulus C (see Fig. 14 ) showed two ways users could learn why a response received a particular confidence rating. The first example, an explanatory bottom-sheet, showed a pop-up that appeared after interacting with the confidence indicator and explained that the confidence rating was based on the quality of the sources. The second example showed source information in the form of an expandable inline dropdown, which users could read without navigating away from the chat interface. Design Stimulus D (see Fig. 15 ) showed three examples of how AI chatbots could provide sources and citations. In the first example, clicking on an in-text citation triggered a pop-up panel containing excerpts from the cited webpage, and the URL to the specific page used to generate the answer. In the second example, specific text was highlighted within the response, and clicking on this text brought up a pop-up panel also containing a URL and excerpts from a relevant webpage. In the third example, a bubble underneath the main response which read ‘Researched’ could be clicked which would dropdown to reveal the number of sources consulted and an overview of the source. Figure 1. Designs of confidence indicators shown to interview participants (Design Stimulus A) 3.1.4. Data analysis. We followed an inductive thematic analysis approach. The first author read the interview transcripts to familiarise themselves with the data. They then conducted the primary analysis using a bottom-up coding process. After coding four interviews, the first author iteratively compared codes across participants and grouped related codes into broader conceptual categories (e.g., ‘verification cues’ or ‘high-stakes contexts’), before coding the next 1-2 interviews, repeating the process until all transcripts had been analysed. The broader research team then discussed the emerging concepts, reviewing and refining the category structure and iterating over larger themes until consensus was reached regarding the key final themes. 3.2. Findings Our analysis surfaced insights into how participants used and interpreted confidence and source indicators, how these features impacted their verification behaviour, as well as how their use and perceptions of these indicators was shaped by contextual factors such as topic, stakes, and complexity. 3.2.1. Confidence indicators Participants agreed that knowing how confident a chatbot was in its response would be beneficial. Specifically, participants mentioned using confidence indicators as cues to determine when they could rely on an answer and when additional verification might be required. For example, several participants described confidence indicators as a cue for deciding whether to perform further fact-checking or search for information independently. One participant explained that confidence could help determine “how much research I should put in myself” (P7). Confidence was therefore viewed by some people less as a direct measure of truth and more as a guide for allocating verification effort. Participants also frequently described confidence indicators as useful for aligning their expectations with model accuracy: “it’s good to know that you can recognize… that the system can recognize whether it’s fully accurate or not and if it’s very confident or not.” (P3) Participants often felt that low-confidence indicators would prepare them for possible inaccuracies and reduce disappointment if an answer proved incorrect. As P5 explained: “at least I understood that it was low confidence and it was incorrect.” Similarly, P1 interpreted low-confidence signalling as an act of transparency: “They’re like, you can’t trust what we say, but we want to let you at least know we’re trying.” In contrast, participants reacted strongly to imagined scenarios where confidence indicators were incorrect. While low confidence paired with a correct answer was generally viewed as confusing but acceptable, high confidence paired with an incorrect answer was perceived as a serious issue that eroded participants’ trust and would discourage future use of the system. As P7 stated: “I’ll be very mad. And I would probably not use AI again.” Communicating confidence Although participants unanimously agreed on the importance of knowing how confident a chatbot was in its responses, many differing definitions and interpretations of confidence emerged during the interviews. Some participants described percentage confidence as the probability that the AI’s response was correct, while others conceptualised it as the proportion of the response that was accurate, or the proportion of the response that was based on the source that it cited. As P7 explained: “So it’s kind of giving off the idea, well, to me that it’s 100% accurate to what the source said.” One participant expressed the belief that high confidence meant that the AI system had already performed verification on their behalf: “Because if you tell me like, you’re very confident your answers, I know, okay, you double-checked, you verified. So I wouldn’t need to do that” (P3). Interestingly, several participants shifted between different interpretations of confidence during the same interview, i.e., their descriptions of how they interpreted AI confidence suggested multiple, conflicting mental models of what this confidence represented. These findings suggest that confidence indicators may be susceptible to multiple competing mental models, creating ambiguity around their intended meaning. Participants also frequently highlighted that they expected explanations describing how confidence scores were generated, and what information they were based on. P7 suggested making uncertainty more concrete by highlighting certain parts of the AI response that were less confident: “a disclaimer at the bottom saying like a percent or sentence saying I feel this is […] 100 confident, 50 confident, or highlights or bolds the parts and saying bolded parts, please fact-check.” Presentation and Context Most participants preferred numerical confidence percentages over categorical labels such as ‘high’ or ‘low’ confidence. Numerical values were perceived as more ‘exact’ and precise. However, this preference was not universal. Some participants argued that percentages were inherently vague because they did not explain how the values had been calculated or what exactly they represented. Participants generally agreed that AI confidence was particularly important for high stakes information, such as “health or career related finances” (P1). Several participants also distinguished between simple and complex queries. For straightforward questions with clear answers, categorical indicators such as ‘high confidence’ were often considered sufficient. However, for nuanced or consequential topics, participants preferred numerical confidence estimates that provided additional detail. For example, P7 stated: “since it’s a drug and relates to health, I would prefer like I would feel more safe and trusting if it said the percent. Because you know […] if it were my health, I wouldn’t just want to be high confidence, I would want it to be 100%” (P7) Similarly, the same participant suggested that percentages become more useful as questions become more complex: “I think it really depends what I’m asking for, how much research goes into the question. If it’s just a one sided question, then yeah, I would like high confidence. But since this is an in-depth question, there are a lot of aspects, I do like the percent level.” Although participants valued confidence indicators, many argued that confidence information alone was insufficient. Instead, participants frequently requested accompanying sources that would allow them to understand why a response received a particular confidence score and independently assess its credibility. Confidence indicators were therefore often interpreted as a signal to inspect supporting evidence rather than as evidence in themselves. 3.2.2. Source indicators Participants generally viewed sources as useful, and in some cases, crucial elements to accompany AI responses. Sources served several functions: they acted as proof for claims, provided tangible evidence that could be inspected directly, and helped users determine whether information was trustworthy. As P5 explained: “I just like having sources and like just showing proof of like what it’s mentioning.” Similarly, P1 described the importance of having information that users could explore further for themselves: “Having an article, something to click on, something to learn more information about, something to pinpoint more.” Several participants also interpreted sources as evidence that the AI system had actively gathered supporting information. As P7 noted: “But with the link it makes it seem like they actually went in and did research to formulate this answer.” Source credibility Participants referred to a variety of source types when describing credibility, including mainstream news organisations, government websites, and academic research papers. Credibility was also linked to reputation and prior experience. P1 described relying on collective judgments, and reputation built over time to assess source quality: “From […] people that used the sources before, people that know what it’s about […] Knowing people used it before, knowing that it’s provided accuracy for years.” However, participants varied in how many sources they considered sufficient to accompany a response. For example, some participants took the view that “the more sources the better” or that “at least 10 good sources” might be appropriate. Others believed that “one source is enough”, provided it was credible. P5 emphasised the importance of source diversity, suggesting that AI responses should include: “three different places, three different sources.” Limitations of sources Despite placing high importance on the role of sources in assessing AI factuality, participants also identified several concerns about providing sources alongside AI responses. First, checking sources can require considerable effort. While sources provide opportunities for verification, many participants acknowledged that they may not always take the time required to inspect them: “Yeah, I’ll click on it, but then let’s say I’m in a rush. I probably would not want to because then I would have to do extra work to like, probably [check] the information myself.” (P3) Second, participants expressed concerns about retrieval accuracy. Some participants had experienced doubts regarding whether an AI system had correctly interpreted their queries and selected relevant information. P1 expressed uncertainty about whether the system would retrieve the appropriate content: “If they interpreted my answer right, if they look up for the right information.” P7 observed that AI inaccuracy, despite there being correct answers available online, was particularly frustrating: “There are accurate answers all over the Internet … and it’s giving me inaccurate responses, then I’d prefer just to go to the source itself.” Third, participants were sceptical regarding whether AI systems could reliably provide genuine sources. Several participants described past experiences where AI systems generated fabricated or inaccessible source links. As P7 explained: “Because in my experience I got sources and links that led to fake websites or websites that didn’t exist.” Context and presentation Participants described how task context influenced how likely they were to check sources. Academic work and healthcare questions were frequently identified as situations where sources would be particularly beneficial: “People that’s like maybe doing a project or something for college or, you know, they want definitely accurate information.” (P1) Participants also had clear preferences regarding source presentation. Participants tended to prefer dropdown designs over pop-up ones, mentioning that sources should be easy to locate, directly accessible, and connected to specific claims within the AI response. Participants also preferred designs that presented excerpts or pull quotes from source material because these reduced the effort required to verify information and helped identify potential hallucinations: “it’s saying exactly which part was taken from the source” (P7). Rather than simply providing links, participants wanted transparency about exactly which information was being used to support a claim. The analysis of the semi-structured interviews provided rich insights into how laypeople use AI chatbots for information-seeking in their everyday lives. Building on these qualitative findings, in the next section, we developed a survey and collected data from a large U.S. representative sample, in order to gain broader understanding of how people evaluate AI factuality. 4.
